mathcounts-sample-school-target-01.prompt: Charles has opened a service, called Charlie’s Chores, that performs various household chores for families in his neighborhood. The table shows the amount he charges for each chore and how many times he was hired to complete that chore in January. How much money in dollars did Charlie’s Chores earn in the month of January?

mathcounts-sample-school-target-02.prompt: Sunil draws a regular hexagon and a convex quadrilateral on a sheet of paper, so that no side of the quadrilateral lies on the same line as a side of the hexagon. What is the maximum total number of points in which the sides of the quadrilateral can intersect the sides of the hexagon?

mathcounts-sample-school-target-03.prompt: Penelope and George go trick-or-treating together. Penelope gets 152 pieces of candy and George gets 124 pieces of candy. Penelope eats 5 pieces of candy every day, and George eats 4 pieces of candy every day. After how many days will George have the same amount of candy as Penelope?

mathcounts-sample-school-target-04.prompt: Rosie grows 160 bushels of corn per acre in a right triangular field, as shown, with perpendicular sides of lengths 660 feet and 1320 feet. Given that an acre equals 43,560 ft$^2$, what is the total number of bushels of corn that Rosie grows?

mathcounts-sample-school-target-05.prompt: A standard, six-sided die is rolled five times. What is the probability that the five rolls are either all the same or all different? Express your answer to the nearest hundredth of a percent.

mathcounts-sample-school-target-06.prompt: If $(0, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(-2, 6)$ and $(a, b)$ are the coordinates of the vertices of a parallelogram, what is the least possible value for $a + b$?

mathcounts-sample-school-target-07.prompt: Alan, Ben and Craig, who have three distinct ages, are among five children running a race. Assuming there are no ties, in how many different orders can the five children finish the race with Alan, Ben and Craig in order from oldest to youngest?

mathcounts-sample-school-target-08.prompt: Let a *trime* be defined as a three-digit integer for which any two digits of the integer, ordered as they appear in the original integer, form a two-digit prime number. For example, 137 is a trime because 13, 17 and 37 are all prime numbers. However, 211 is not a trime because 21 is not prime. What is the greatest trime?
